American plaice (Hippoglossoides platessoides) females reach an ultimate total length of 82.6 centimeters [Li = 82.6 centimeters], making this flatfish one of the larger members of the Pleuronectidae family in the North Atlantic. This maximum size is attained only after many years of sustained somatic growth, with the largest specimens typically captured from the deeper, colder portions of their geographic range. In contrast, the length at puberty for females is considerably smaller, with individuals initiating gonad maturation once they have reached 35 centimeters [Lp = 35 centimeters]. This pronounced difference between the size at which reproduction begins and the ultimate possible length suggests a life-history strategy wherein females invest heavily in somatic growth well beyond the onset of reproductive activity, a pattern commonly observed among flatfishes inhabiting high-latitude continental shelves.

The age at birth for American plaice, measured as the interval between egg fertilization and eclosion, has been determined under controlled laboratory conditions. At a stable water temperature of 5.6 °C [T = 5.6 °C], the incubation period for the fertilized ova lasts approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days]. This relatively brief developmental window is characteristic of demersal eggs spawned in cold boreal waters, where the metabolic costs of prolonged incubation could increase the risk of predation on the yolk-laden embryos. The newly emerged prolarvae at hatching possess a wet weight at birth of 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams], a value that can be approximated from the mean egg diameter of 3 millimeters. This extremely small body mass underscores the highly fecund, low-investment-per-offspring reproductive mode typical of many marine teleosts.

Female American plaice exhibit a maximum reproductive rate that has been quantified through field studies of spawning frequency and batch fecundity. Under thermal conditions of 5.6 °C [T = 5.6 °C], ripe females are capable of producing approximately 1 batch of eggs per day [F_R_i = approximately 1 batch of eggs per day] over the course of the spawning season, and each batch contains an average of 367 eggs [N_R_i = each batch contains an average of 367 eggs]. This daily output results in an exceptionally high annual fecundity that compensates for the high mortality rates experienced during the planktonic larval phase. The wet weight at puberty, which corresponds to the body mass attained when females first become capable of sustaining this reproductive effort, has been estimated at 342 grams [Wwp = 342 grams].

The ultimate wet weight of female American plaice is derived from length-weight relationships fitted to extensive survey data. Using the established morphometric conversion of 0.00646 times total length raised to the 3.06 power, an individual measuring 82.6 centimeters in total length is predicted to have a body mass of 4700 grams [Wwi = 4700 grams]. Reaching this asymptotic mass requires decades of continuous feeding on a diet dominated by benthic invertebrates and small fishes. The species' maximum lifespan is notable among flatfishes, with the oldest documented individuals surviving for 30 years [am = 30 years] when reared at temperatures near 5.6 °C [T = 5.6 °C]. This extended longevity allows ample time for iteroparous reproduction across many successive spawning seasons.

Comparisons with congeneric species highlight the relatively slow life-history pace of American plaice. Whereas related Pleuronectes species from more southerly latitudes often mature earlier and at smaller body sizes, Hippoglossoides platessoides delays the onset of reproductive activity, investing those additional years into achieving a larger body mass before first spawning. Field surveys consistently demonstrate that females attain puberty at 35 centimeters [Lp = 35 centimeters] total length, a threshold that corresponds to a corresponding wet weight at puberty of approximately 342 grams [Wwp = approximately 342 grams]. The ecological drivers of this strategy are likely rooted in the cold, low-productivity waters of the Grand Banks and the Gulf of St. Lawrence, where slow growth and high adult survival favor delayed reproduction in favor of increased fecundity at larger body sizes, a pattern that aligns with predictions from life-history theory for long-lived marine fishes.
